name: African black soap
what_people_do: Wash the face and body, and sometimes hair, with a soft soap made from plantain-skin and cocoa-pod ash with palm oil and shea; known as dudu osun or ose dudu.
why_they_say_it_works: Said to clear acne, soothe eczema and fade marks, and to be gentler than shop soap.

documented_by.source: Ogunbiyi A, Enechukwu NA 2021, PMID 33571401 (narrative review of African black soap)
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Narrative review by Nigerian dermatologists: the soap is traditional and widely used; they state "some of the claims remain anecdotal"; lab studies show antimicrobial action against Staphylococcus and some Streptococcus. I did not open a survey of how people use it.

evidence.population: Laboratory studies cited in the review
evidence.finding: Activity against Staphylococcus and some Streptococcus; does not establish benefit for acne, eczema or scars.

source.name: Ogunbiyi A, Enechukwu NA 2021, PMID 33571401 (narrative review of African black soap)

evidence.tested: Black soap on skin in people

source.name: agent4-traditional-practices.md, 12 Nov 2026 (research file in this project)

harm_note: Soaps are alkaline and can dry or irritate sensitive or eczema-prone skin (general dermatology, not from the review abstract).
